newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds fall, dollar up on rate speculation.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds fall, dollar up on rate speculation.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks and bonds fell Tuesday after a Federal Reserve official fuelled speculation that interest rates may soon rise.
The dollar rose to eight-week highs against the German mark and Japanese yen as higher U.S. rates would make dollar-based assets more attractive to investors.
In commodity markets, soybean futures surged on concern that freezing temperatures were expected in Midwestern growing regions, and crude oil prices were higher as tension flared again in Iraq.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended off 6.66 points at 5,727.18 after gaining a total of 127 points on Monday and Friday.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,145 to 1,137 on active volume of 371 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Analysts said the market's bullish tone in the wake of Friday's August payrolls report, which allayed Wall Street's worst inflation fears, was dampened by Fed Gov. Janet Yellen's comment that the economy was at a critical point.
"We're in an inflationary danger zone," Yellen told Reuters in an interview. "There's definitely a chance inflation will rise."

Her cautious comments suggested that she might be willing to support a quarter percentage point rise in short-term interest rates at the Fed's next policy-making meeting on Sept. 24 to help ensure against higher inflation.
Analysts said they were impressed with the stock market's performance, noting that investors have been pricing in a rise in short-term interest rates after a series of strong economic reports.
"Stocks have rallied in the past two days. So far this first day of a pullback looks awfully good given what's happening to bonds," said Ralph Bloch, chief technical analyst at Raymond James.
In treasury markets, The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond closed at 95-17/32, off 15/32 on the day to yield 7.11 percent vs. 7.07 percent on Monday.

"The Yellen comments were the catalyst," said Lee Youngdahl, money market economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co Inc. "You may get (some FOMC members) on the dissenting side, but it seems like the core consensus is beginning to form around a 25 basis point (one-quarter percentage point) cautionary move."

In foreign exchange markets, the dollar rose to nearly 110 yen and 1.5110 marks, its highest level against both currencies since July 16. Late Tuesday, the dollar fetched 109.85 yen and 1.5110 marks, up from 1.5003 and 109.25 yen late Monday.
The Yellen statements also were a factor in foreign exchange, since higher interest rates would make the dollar a more attractive investment in relation to other currencies.

The dollar also derived strength from Monday's remarks by Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke, who said German overnight lending rates could fall if money supply growth slowed further and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, who said central bankers of the Group of 10 big industrial nations agreed a strong dollar was in everyone's interest.
At the Chicago Baord of Trade, soybeans for November delivery rose 13-1/4 cents to $8.07 a bushel.
Crude oil traded at the New York Mercantile Exchange rose 39 cents to $24.12 per barrel.
London's FTSE 100 closed up 5.3 points at 3,916.1. In Tokyo, the key 225-share Nikkei average gained 357.32 points to close at 20,559.59.
